item.title: Background-free and laser-ionization minimized single-shot fs-EFISH in luminous pulsed plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2611.13158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces spectrally tuned electric field induced second harmonic (t-EFISH) generation for substantially reducing or eliminating background plasma emission in single-shot, time-resolved, electric field measurements. The technique is demonstrated using a femtosecond 1240 nm pump and 620 nm signal detection to avoid spectral and temporal overlap with the early, intense onset of N2(C-B) emission in nanosecond atmospheric-pressure air spark discharges. This enhances signal-to-emission ratios pre- and post-breakdown, enables lower pump energies, suppresses detector saturation, and reduces the coefficient of variation in the electric field measurements by 8.5x. This strategy also provides a pathway for background-free measurements in other discharge environments with varying spectro-temporal emission characteristics. Moreover, the longer 1240 nm pump wavelength reduces multiphoton intrusiveness, directly improving measurement fidelity.
item.dc:creator: Vidyadhara B. V. Kumar, Karna Patel, Aman Satija, Sally Bane, Terrence R. Meyer

item.title: High-power X-Point Target divertor experiments on the TCV tokamak
item.description: arXiv:2611.13179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stationary power exhaust in the X-Point Target (XPT) divertor configuration is investigated in high-power ($2.5\,\text{MW}$) TCV L-mode discharges, in which the Lengyel detachment scaling metric $P_{\text{SOL}}B_{0}/(R_{0}n_{e,\text{u}}^{2})$ lies in the range expected for reactors (SPARC, ITER, ARC). Compared with a conventional single-null (SN) divertor, the XPT improves power exhaust performance, reducing the peak outer target heat flux by 40--60\% and enabling divertor detachment with nitrogen seeding under conditions in which the SN cannot be detached. Detachment evolves asymmetrically across the multiple XPT outer strike points. The sensitivities of the peak target heat fluxes and impurity emission front positions to the X-point separation ($\text{d}R_{\text{u},X2}$) are characterized and found to decrease at higher nitrogen seeding levels. Field-reversal experiments reveal the critical role of $E\times B$ drifts inherent to the magnetic topology of the secondary X-point, which drive an unconventional redistribution of density and impurity radiation in the XPT divertor and thereby cause the asymmetries between the XPT outer strike points, largely confirming the expectations from recent SOLPS-ITER modelling. A framework for understanding the power exhaust physics of the XPT is presented, detailing the roles of SOL splitting, connection length peaking, $E\times B$ drifts, and vessel geometry. Together, these results establish an experimental physics basis for the XPT divertor as a potential power exhaust solution for tokamak reactors.

item.title: Drive and damping govern resonant electron energy redistribution in a kinetic model informed by helium discharges
item.description: arXiv:2611.13587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energetic electrons exchange energy with electrostatic waves in low-temperature plasmas, but wave amplitude alone does not determine the direction or cumulative effect of that exchange. We analyse nonlinear electron redistribution using a single-mode kinetic model parameterized by published helium-discharge measurements. Frequency and pressure comparisons are combined with a controlled damping scan and explicit particle-current and energy diagnostics. Across the frequency cases, the inferred resonant drive varies by a factor of 2.7 while background damping varies by only about 9%. Reducing pressure from 33.3 to 10.66 Pa at 37 MHz increases the net drive by a factor of 2.24. In the damping scan, the peak wave energy and residual parallel-energy deficit both decrease by approximately 93%, consistent with quadratic field-amplitude scaling at the reported endpoints. An integrated energy identity connects retained wave energy, background loss and distribution recovery, and distinguishes cessation of wave growth from reversal of energy transfer. Quantitative timescale and directional-distribution tests define the connection between this reduced model and discharge kinetics. The analysis provides a common interpretation of resonant redistribution, coherent current and energy exchange, together with observables for testing that interpretation in kinetic simulations and phase-resolved measurements.
item.dc:creator: Zhao-Ju Bo, Lei Chang, Shi-Jie Zhang, Ying-Xin Zhao, Zi-Chen Kan, Ji-Kai Sun, Ilya Zadiriev, Elena Kralkina, Shin-Jae You, Jing-Jing Ma, G\'eza Husi

item.title: Analytic Solution to Cumulative Coulomb Scattering in Boltzmann Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.13793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In plasmas, frequent soft Coulomb collisions gradually transfer energy and momentum, whereas a single close collision can change both abruptly and redirect a particle. This coexistence can shape runaway-electron avalanches in tokamaks and alpha-particle heating in inertial fusion, yet no first-principles analytic theory has determined how the cumulative statistics evolve under plasma conditions. Fokker--Planck and moment-matched models reproduce average transport but do not determine how scattering evolves from isolated events to cumulative relaxation across plasma conditions. Here we resolve this long-standing problem directly from Boltzmann theory. By asymptotically rescaling the exact angular expansion, we obtain the first quantitative map of the single-collision, core-tail coexistence, and low-order relaxation regimes within a unified Boltzmann framework. The rescaling also provides explicit analytic representations of the angular distribution across these regimes without empirical transition parameters. The theory further shows that small-angle models differ from the Boltzmann distribution even in the forward core, so appending a large-angle tail to a conventional core cannot recover the collision statistics. In fast-electron transport, this full-range redistribution leaves mean energy loss nearly unchanged yet counterintuitively enhances beam concentration and modifies the energy flux delivered to a finite region.
item.dc:creator: Tie-Huai Zhang, Wei-Min Wang, Zi-Yan Zhang, Yu-Tong Li, Jie Zhang

item.title: Filamentary dynamics in fan-like structures in high-altitude lightning discharges
item.description: arXiv:2611.14193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present LOFAR radio telescope measurements revealing that high-altitude negative leaders (HANLs) exhibit behavior completely different from the current paradigm of negative leader propagation. Our data show that the fan at the tip of a propagating HANL is formed by filaments that behave like smoothly advancing negative leaders. These negative leader filaments appear to have moderate conductivity, remain thin (radius $\sim1$ m), grow continuously at $\sim10^5$ m/s over hundreds of meters, and emit VHF radiation persistently. The observations show that the filaments making up the fan in front of a propagating negative leader are not necessarily streamers, as commonly assumed. Previous work suggesting to observe streamers at the tips of negative leaders should be re-examined in light of these new findings
item.dc:creator: M. A. A. Lourens, B. M. Hare, O. Scholten, S. Cummer, J. Dwyer, N. Liu, C. Sterpka, P. Turekova, B. Wu, S. ter Veen

item.title: Compact plasma-based extreme compression of relativistic electron beams
item.description: arXiv:2611.13436v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accelerated particle beams are essential tools of modern science and technology with applications ranging from medicine [1], to light sources [2], to high-energy physics [3]. Over time, as accelerator-based experiments become more sophisticated and probe natural phenomena with greater temporal resolution, there is an increasing demand on beam parameters, in particular on bunch duration. Experiments have been proposed that require beams with 1-2 orders of magnitude shorter durations than what is possible with current state-of-the-art technology. However, state-of-the-art temporal bunch compressors force a trade-off between how short an electron bunch can be made and how well its transverse quality survives the strong bending magnets required to do so -- a limitation that stands as a grand challenge for accelerator physics to-date [4]. In this experiment, we demonstrate a new, compact compression technique for generating ultrashort, high-peak-current electron bunches that circumvents this trade-off using plasma wakefield acceleration. Just as chirped pulse amplification unlocked ultrashort, high-power laser pulses and the technologies that followed from them, here we demonstrate an analogous chirp-and-compress strategy applied to relativistic electron beams by using the extreme electric fields of a plasma wakefield in place of a stretcher-amplifier, thereby unlocking the path to ultrashort, extremely high-current electron beams. We demonstrate the first application of this plasma-compressed bunch using it to drive single-microbunch free electron lasing at optical wavelengths in a single, meter-scale undulator module, producing radiation pulses roughly four orders of magnitude more energetic than the first beam-driven, plasma-based free electron laser demonstration at the same accelerator facility [5, 6].

item.title: Development of a versatile modular system to study the ablation and plume expansion in a thin film
item.description: arXiv:2611.13570v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time-resolved investigation of laser ablation of thin films requires stable, repeatable, and efficient experimental environment. Conventional approaches often rely on multiple laser-ablation shots acquired at different delay times to reconstruct the temporal evolution of the process, thereby assuming shot-to-shot reproducibility. This work presents a novel modular experimental setup that addresses these challenges and enables a systematic pump--probe study of laser--matter interaction. The setup provides reliable single-pulse measurements with controlled sample positioning inside the high vacuum chamber, as well as integrated data recording, which improves redundancy and ease with which experiments can be performed. Further, the setup serves as an advanced diagnostic tool for investigating the time evolution of laser--matter interactions, ablation dynamics and laser-produced plasmas in a single laser shot, in various configurations with a temporal resolution better than 15 ns. Using this capability, we show that for a fixed ablation geometry, the transient reflectivity and transmission response depends strongly on the probing side, indicating that probing direction is an independent diagnostic variable whose omission can lead to incomplete or misleading picture of the ablation dynamics. This experimental technique can advance the understanding of surface modification and plume expansion, which are relevant to fundamental studies and also for range of applications, including laser cleaning of tokamak viewports and mirrors, pulsed laser deposition (PLD), surface structuring and laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT), among others. The present setup is versatile enough to perform these studies under different ablation configurations without implementing major changes in the experimental configuration.
item.dc:creator: Renjith Kumar R, Pabitra Kumar Mishra, B R Geethika, Hem C Joshi, Jinto Thomas

item.title: Nucleation of water ice under weak ionization via clustering on negative ions
item.description: arXiv:2611.14441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Water-ice grains are shown to form spontaneously in a cold, weakly-ionized laboratory plasma with trace water admixture when neutrals and ions are cooled below $\sim$200 K. These conditions serve as an analog of ice nucleation in cold astrophysical and atmospheric environments. The ice grains form without the presence of particulate impurities, and do not form in the absence of ionization, indicating that nucleation is induced by ions. Time-resolved ion mass spectrometry provides separate detection of clusters of water molecules on both positive and negative ions. Hydrated negative ions, mainly $\mathrm{OH^-(H_2O)_n}$, grow to $\sim$200 amu, while hydrated positive ions, mainly $\mathrm{H^+(H_2O)_n}$, remain small and short-lived. As the temperature is reduced from room temperature toward 200 K, negative ion clusters grow in size and then drop sharply in abundance, consistent with the onset of rapid growth into macroscopic ice grains below a critical temperature. This indicates that hydrated negative ions are key precursors to ice nucleation in cold, weakly ionized environments, such as the Earth's mesosphere and protoplanetary disks, providing a concrete pathway for ice formation in environments where the nucleation mechanism has remained unresolved. This negative ion pathway is estimated to dominate over ice deposition on pre-existing dust grains in protoplanetary disk locations where there is sufficient UV to partially dissociate water molecules, and in addition, where negative ions such as OH- can form readily through electron attachment at low temperature.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'e Nicolov, Efstratios M. Kritikos, William A. Goddard III., Paul M. Bellan

item.title: High-quality electron beam generation from laser wakefield accelerators for driving compact free electron lasers
item.description: arXiv:2501.09916v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite the successful demonstration of compact free electron lasers (FELs) driven by laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs), the pursuit of further enhancements in high-gain compact FELs presents a challenge due to the limitations in electron beam quality. In this work, we pinpoint the pivotal physics and optimization strategies for high-quality single-stage LWFAs that are crucial for high-gain FELs. We have delved into the synergistic injection mechanism, where the self-evolution injection threshold is far from reached at the injection position, with both the shock front and self-evolution of the laser playing a role in the injection process. A thorough discussion has been provided on the beam-quality degradation and optimization strategies, in terms of global (slice) energy spread and projected (slice) emittance. With the goal of achieving high-gain FELs driven by LWFAs, we have also explored the synthesis quality of the electron beam to determine an optimized power gain length. A comprehensive start-to-end simulation has been conducted, demonstrating the effectiveness of compact FELs powered by these high-quality electron beams. The resulting radiation reaches the saturation regime after a 4.5-meter-long undulator, with an energy of 17.4 {\mu}J and a power of 6.0 GW at a wavelength of 23.9 nm. This proposed scheme offers not only a framework for optimizing beam quality in LWFAs, but also a promising path for future compact LWFA-driven FELs to achieve saturated regimes, opening up new possibilities for widespread applications.
item.dc:creator: Ke Feng, Kangnan Jiang, Runshu Hu, Chen Lv, Xizhuan Chen, Hai Jiang, Shixia Luan, Wentao Wang, Ruxin Li

item.title: Self-organisation through layering of $\beta$-plane like turbulence in plasmas and geophysical fluids
item.description: arXiv:2511.10438v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Staircase formation and layering is studied in simplified, potential vorticity conserving models of plasmas and geophysical fluids, by investigating turbulent self-organisation and nonlinear saturation with different mechanisms of free energy production -- forcing or linear instability -- and with standard or modified zonal flow responses. To this end, staircase formation in both the standard and modified Charney-Hasegawa-Mima equations with stochastic forcing, along with two different simple instability driven models -- one from a plasma and from a geophysical context -- are studied and compared. In these studies, it is observed that $\beta$-plane turbulence that does not distinguish between zonal and non-zonal perturbations (i.e., standard zonal response) gradually forms large-scale, elliptic zonal structures that merge progressively, regardless of whether it is driven by forcing (though it should be slow enough to allow wave couplings) or by the baroclinic instability, using for example a two-layer model. Conversely, the plasma system, with its modified zonal response, can rapidly form straight, stationary jets of well-defined size, again regardless of the way it is driven: by stochastic forcing or by the dissipative drift instability. Furthermore, the instability-driven plasma system exhibits a phase transition between a zonal flow dominated state and an eddy dominated state. In both states, saturation is possible without large-scale friction.
item.dc:creator: P. L. Guillon, G. Dif-Pradalier, Y. Sarazin, D. W. Hughes, \"O. D. G\"urcan

item.title: Modeling runaway electron mitigation via passively driven plasma instabilities in a high-current tokamak
item.description: arXiv:2611.04906v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A critical challenge for tokamak-based fusion power plants is the formation of high-current, relativistic runaway electron (RE) beams during abrupt confinement loss events called disruptions. RE beams may significantly damage machine components if left unmitigated, jeopardizing the operational and economic viability of fusion power plants. We present the first self-consistent extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) computational study of RE mitigation with a passively driven RE mitigation coil (REMC) in a high-current tokamak. RE generation and transport are coupled with REMC-driven MHD activity in a 3D simulation that models the thermal and current quench phases of a mid-plane disruption, together with the vertical displacement and final termination of the plasma and RE beam on SPARC -- a high-field, high-current tokamak designed to achieve a fusion gain Q > 1. We demonstrate that REMC-driven magnetic stochasticity can reduce the RE current by over an order-of-magnitude when compared to unmitigated disruptions. The final termination is mediated via a post-thermal-quench "cold" vertical displacement of the plasma, which, together with magnetic stochasticity, increases RE losses via scrape-off once the plasma contacts the first wall. These results demonstrate a viable mechanism for RE mitigation using passively driven plasma instabilities on high-current tokamaks.
item.dc:creator: R Datta, C Clauser, G Hu, A Braun, N Ferraro, R Sweeney, R A Tinguely

item.title: Stability and optical quality of "windmill"-formed 8CB liquid crystal films for replenishable plasma mirrors
item.description: arXiv:2509.18448v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquid crystal (LC) film plasma mirrors (PMs) based on 4-octyl-4'-cyanobiphenyl (8CB) are an enabling technology for reflecting high-fluence laser pulses. These freestanding LC films can achieve high optical quality and are well-suited for rep-rated applications, as motorized devices continuously replenish films over an aperture following each destructive laser shot. However, a systematic characterization of film quality as a function of seminal operating conditions had not yet been performed for the LC "windmill" version of the device, which aims to match the repetition rate of an existing "spinning disk" (SDI) version and the angular stability of the "linear slider" (LSTI) version. We determined the 8CB film quality using low-power wavefront measurements, and studied the film-to-film wavefront stability and formation reliability. The film-formation reliability of 8CB LC films demonstrated 97\% formation success at 2.7 mm/s film-forming speeds, but decreased to 45\% at 10.8 mm/s. These reliability numbers will inform future designs to reach Hz-level repetition rates and beyond. Depending on area-of-interest within the 10 mm diameter film, the added wavefront root-mean-squared (RMS) variation was as small as 10 nm for a 2 mm diameter region, and $<$50 nm for a 3 mm diameter region. Within the optimal 21-22$^\circ$C operating regime, pointing fluctuations remained at or below 0.52 mrad. With a maximum effective film formation frequency of \textasciitilde0.25 Hz, these results establish windmill-formed 8CB films as promising candidates to pursue next-iteration improvements towards rep-rated plasma-mirror operation.

item.title: Radiation damage to normal mammalian tissue in vivo with laser-driven protons at ultra-high instantaneous dose rate
item.description: arXiv:2602.20460v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The differential sparing of normal tissues relative to tumor control observed at ultra-high dose rates, referred to as the FLASH effect, has recently gained considerable attention. The therapeutic advantages of FLASH radiotherapy are expected to be further amplified through the use of protons and ions, which enable precise dose deposition at tumor depth while minimizing irradiation of healthy tissues proximal and distal to the target. Nevertheless, the mechanism underlying this sparing effect remains poorly understood. Laser-driven proton accelerators are capable of delivering uniquely high instantaneous dose rates in ultrashort bunches. Here, we report the first in vivo investigation of normal tissue response to laser-driven proton irradiation, with exposures to 8 MeV protons, delivering total doses up to 51 Gy at 2 Gy per laser shot. Our findings reveal a reduction in tissue swelling following laser-driven proton treatment compared with X-ray irradiations at conventional dose rates. RNA sequencing identified differential gene expression associated with immune and epidermal programs following laser-driven proton irradiations at two different dose levels.
item.dc:creator: Lieselotte Obst-Huebl, Jamie L. Inman, Jared De Chant, Kei Nakamura, Sahel Hakimi, Morgan Cole, Hang Chang, Cameron G. R. Geddes, Anthony J. Gonsalves, Jian-Hua Mao, Carl B. Schroeder, Blake A. Simmons, Jeroen van Tilborg, Eric Esarey, Antoine M. Snijders

item.title: Is the Quiet-Sun Heating Requirement Observationally Established?
item.description: arXiv:2607.28530v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How much energy does the quiet corona require? Its radiation shows that energy must be supplied. Electrons also carry heat into or out of it. We ask whether temperature observations justify the heat-flow estimate used to judge a heating mechanism's energy supply. Two radio methods give temperatures near 0.62 and 1.5 million kelvin. A population with extra fast electrons can give both readings. Unresolved structure and delayed ion formation also leave Maxwellian explanations open. Neither temperature interpretation alone determines the heat flow. The tested local conduction formula diverges for the idealized fast-electron model with an unbroken tail. Applying X-ray limits to the model still leaves about 5--6% of the electrons holding 28--33% of its kinetic energy. The heat they carry depends on the balance between directions and on conditions along their paths. Source and collision calculations test whether the population could be sustained. The observations examined here do not establish whether the conductive estimate is accurate enough for the heating comparison. We cannot judge whether a mechanism supplies enough energy against a heat loss we have not established. Measuring, reliably calculating, or sufficiently bounding that loss would settle this part of the budget.
item.dc:creator: Victor Edmonds

item.title: Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs
item.description: arXiv:2609.02982v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.
item.dc:creator: Qiyun Cheng, Valentin Duruisseaux, Cesar F. Clauser, Md Hossain Sahadath, Huihua Yang, Shaowu Pan, Nathaniel Ferraro, Anima Anandkumar, Wei Ji, Cristina Rea
